summaries.example: Imagine two classrooms learning a new game. One class learns by watching older students, while the other invents its own rules. Soon, the classes may play differently. Their differences could come from what they learned from people, from the places they live, or from their own discoveries. Cognitive science helps us ask which causes matter.
summaries.summary: Culture and cognitive science is about how human thinking is shaped by both minds and social worlds. Cognitive science studies mental activity, learning, language, memory, decisions, and intelligent behavior. It uses ideas and methods from several subjects. One important idea treats thinking as information processing, though other approaches emphasize bodies, environments, actions, and relationships. Culture is harder to define. It can include patterns, habits, knowledge, values, rules, tools, and products. A useful idea in this entry is that culture involves information moving between people and producing lasting changes in behavior. The entry explains why researchers now pay more attention to differences between groups. A large amount of psychological research studied WEIRD participants and sometimes treated their results as facts about everyone. The entry calls for broader and more careful research. It also compares explanations of variation. Some explanations focus on inherited mental abilities and responses to environments. Others focus on information learned from other people. Some combine these possibilities. Human social learning can create cumulative culture: later people keep, change, and add to what earlier people made. Researchers debate the roles of imitation, teaching, individual discovery, memory, language, imagination, cooperation, and norms. Philosophers help examine the evidence and concepts, and they also use the findings to explore whether minds extend into tools and social settings, how culture shapes mental illness, how moral ideas vary, how groups gain knowledge, and whether philosophers should rely so heavily on their own intuitions.
key_ideas: Cognitive science studies minds as systems that handle information, but researchers disagree about exactly how this happens.
Culture has many meanings. In this field, it often means information passed between people that changes behavior for a lasting time.
People in different groups may think and act differently because of social learning, individual learning, environments, biology, or combinations of these.
Much psychological research used participants from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic societies. The WEIRD challenge asks whether those participants really represent all humans.
Humans can copy, teach, invent, and improve ideas across generations. Researchers debate which mental abilities make this possible.
Philosophers use research about culture to rethink minds, knowledge, morality, mental health, and the methods of philosophy.
summaries.why_it_matters: The way people think is connected to the people and places around them. Studying culture can help us avoid treating one group’s habits as the human rule. It can also show how teaching, cooperation, tools, and shared knowledge help communities solve problems. Learning about these questions encourages curiosity and care when we compare different ways of living and thinking.

important_terms.definition: A group of fields that study minds, thinking, learning, and intelligent behavior. It brings together psychology, philosophy, language study, computer science, anthropology, and brain science.
Information, habits, skills, beliefs, rules, and objects that people learn from others and pass along in a community.
Learning by watching, listening to, or working with other people or animals instead of figuring everything out alone.
A change that is kept, improved, and built upon by later generations. Human tools and knowledge often grow this way.
The idea that parts of thinking may be helped by things outside the brain, such as notes, tools, technology, or other people.

questions_to_think_about: When you learn a game from friends, which parts did you discover and which parts did others pass to you?
Can one group of people represent all human beings in a study?
Is copying always the best way to learn?
Can a notebook, phone, or teacher become part of the way someone thinks?

summaries.example: Suppose a researcher tests memory using students from one wealthy, highly educated society and finds that they organize information in a particular way. The result may reveal something about memory, but it may also reflect schooling, technology, language, or local expectations. A cross-cultural project might combine experiments with ethnographic work to test whether the pattern is widespread, culturally variable, or produced by an interaction between cognitive mechanisms and social environments.
summaries.summary: The entry examines how culture has become central to cognitive science and to philosophy of mind and science. Cognitive science is presented as an interdisciplinary project concerned with minds, mental organization, and intelligent behavior. Its influential information-processing framework has often used the computer analogy, but computationalism is not the only option: connectionist, embodied, enactive, dynamic-systems, complexity, and predictive approaches challenge or extend classical assumptions. Culture is even less settled as a concept. In one influential account, cultural information is transmitted between people or groups and produces lasting behavioral change. This account emphasizes origin, transmission, and effects rather than content alone. The entry then considers variation between groups. The WEIRD challenge argues that psychology has frequently studied a narrow population and generalized from it to humanity. This creates problems for both sampling and theory, because it leaves the range and causes of cognitive variation poorly understood. Competing explanations appeal to ecological circumstances, evolved psychological mechanisms, individual learning, and socially transmitted information. Evolutionary Psychology often emphasizes evoked responses to environments, while dual-inheritance approaches emphasize cultural inheritance; cultural epidemiology emphasizes how cognitive mechanisms reconstruct and stabilize representations. The entry stresses that these programs may explain different phenomena and can sometimes be combined. A major theme is cumulative culture, in which inherited practices are retained, modified, and expanded. key_ideas: Cognitive science has a shared but non-canonical framework rather than a single theory. Computational, connectionist, embodied, enactive, dynamic, complexity-based, and predictive approaches offer different accounts of information processing.
Culture is conceptually plural. The entry treats socially transmitted information as one influential framework while recognizing that no single definition serves every explanatory purpose.

Explanations of group variation differ over the roles of genes, ecology, individual learning, evolved psychological mechanisms, and transmitted culture. These approaches can overlap rather than form a simple either-or choice.
The WEIRD challenge is both methodological and theoretical: narrow samples can distort claims about human universals and hide the mechanisms that produce psychological diversity.
Cumulative culture raises disputes about imitation, replication, reconstruction, cultural complexity, and the cognitive capacities needed for knowledge and skills to build across generations.
Cultural cognitive science changes philosophical debates about externalism, psychiatry, morality, epistemology, and the evidential status of philosophical intuitions.
summaries.why_it_matters: The cultural turn matters because claims about cognition are also claims about whose minds count as evidence. It encourages researchers to separate universal features from local patterns and to combine methods when experiments alone are insufficient. It also shows that cognition may depend on social and material scaffolding, while raising difficult questions about responsibility, knowledge, moral judgment, psychiatric classification, and the proper methods of philosophy.

important_terms.definition: An interdisciplinary research program studying minds, mental organization, and intelligent behavior through psychology, philosophy, linguistics, computer science, anthropology, economics, evolutionary theory, neuroscience, and related fields.

A contested concept often treated in this field as information transmitted among individuals or groups that produces durable changes in behavior. Other approaches emphasize patterns, functions, products, power, or membership.
The movement of information or behavior between individuals through interaction. It may involve learning, imitation, teaching, communication, and selective attention to particular models.
Cultural change in which later generations preserve, modify, improve, and extend what they inherit, allowing complexity to accumulate over time.
The research challenge created by relying heavily on participants from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic societies and generalizing their results to humanity as a whole.
The view that some cognitive processes or mental contents depend partly on structures outside the individual, including tools, social practices, technology, and culturally organized environments.
A proposed process in which learners reconstruct what they encounter rather than simply copying it, with features of human cognition tending to stabilize some cultural forms.

questions_to_think_about: What evidence would justify moving from a result about one population to a claim about human nature?
Are social learning and individual learning genuinely separate, given that human environments are often designed by other people?
Does cumulative culture require high-fidelity imitation, or can innovation and reconstruction also preserve useful traditions?
If a reasoning tendency is unhelpful for an individual but beneficial for a group, how should it be evaluated?
How should philosophers respond when intuitions vary across cultures, languages, or levels of training?

summaries.example: Imagine a school where students learn a complicated robot-building technique. One student invents a useful shortcut. Others copy it, but each group changes it a little. Over many years, the technique may become much more advanced than anything one student could invent alone. Researchers would ask how much of the result came from individual discovery, imitation, teaching, the school’s tools, and the rules that guided learning.
summaries.summary: Culture and Cognitive Science explores the growing effort to understand minds as both biological and culturally situated. Cognitive science is an interdisciplinary approach involving areas such as psychology, philosophy, linguistics, computer science, anthropology, economics, evolutionary theory, and neuroscience. Many researchers describe mental activity as information processing, often using a computer comparison between physical systems and programs. However, other approaches emphasize connections among brains, bodies, environments, actions, and social settings. The meaning of culture is also disputed. Academic definitions focus on different features, including patterns, processes, products, group membership, and power. For the purposes of much research discussed in the entry, culture can be understood as information transmitted between people or groups that produces lasting behavioral change. The entry gives special attention to variation between groups and to the WEIRD challenge. Psychological research has often relied on participants from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic societies, even though these societies may be unusual in important ways. Treating their results as universal can hide the true range of human cognition and behavior. The entry compares several explanations for variation. Some highlight ecological differences; some emphasize evolved psychological mechanisms that respond flexibly to environments; others focus on cultural inheritance and social learning. Cultural epidemiology adds the idea that learners actively reconstruct what they receive. These explanations are not always strict rivals. key_ideas: Cognitive science uses a shared set of questions and methods, but researchers disagree about whether minds are best understood through computation, embodiment, action, networks, or other models.
There is no universally accepted definition of culture. One important approach focuses on information transmitted socially and its lasting effects on behavior.
Differences between groups may be explained by culture, environment, individual learning, inherited psychology, or interactions among these factors.
The WEIRD challenge questions whether findings from a narrow group of research participants can be treated as universal human facts.
Researchers debate whether cultural change depends mainly on copying, creative reconstruction, teaching, or several processes working together.
Philosophers study how cultural research affects ideas about the mind, morality, knowledge, mental illness, and philosophical evidence.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because culture can influence what people learn, how they reason, how they cooperate, and how they understand themselves. It also affects scientific research itself: the people chosen for studies and the concepts used to measure them can shape conclusions. Studying cultural variation can therefore make psychology and philosophy more accurate, while helping us notice when a local habit has been mistaken for a universal truth.

important_terms.definition: A field that combines several subjects to study thinking, learning, memory, language, decision-making, and intelligent action.
A broad and debated idea covering learned patterns, knowledge, skills, values, rules, objects, and ways of living shared or transmitted by people.
The passing of information or behavior from one person to another through social interaction.
The process by which later people preserve, alter, and build on earlier cultural achievements.
A warning that research based mainly on Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic societies may not describe humans everywhere.
The idea that thinking can be supported, and perhaps sometimes partly constituted, by tools, technology, social practices, and other parts of the environment.
Learning by changing and rebuilding information from what one observes instead of making an exact copy.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a study of one society fail to reveal a universal feature of the mind?
Can a behavior be both individually learned and socially influenced?
What is gained, and what is lost, when cultural information is copied inaccurately?
Should a tool such as a calendar count as part of someone’s thinking or merely as help for thinking?
Could differences in moral judgments show cultural learning, or might they have other causes?
